title: What Are QBTS Stock Investors Overlooking?
detail:
What Are QBTS Stock Investors Overlooking?
Trefis Team

QBTS
IONQ
RGTI
IBM
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) reported revenue of $3.1 million for the second quarter of 2026, a figure essentially flat compared to a year earlier. This stagnation stands out given the $5.4 billion valuation investors have placed on the business, a price that appears to anticipate rapid growth. Underneath the top line, cloud subscriptions and professional services actually expanded at double-digit rates during the period. So why did D-Wave's revenue stand still?

D-Wave Booked Very Little From Selling Computers

The company generated little of its second-quarter revenue from actual quantum computer sales. Systems and other revenue totaled about $300,000 for the period, even though management prices a single annealing system between $20 million and $40 million.

The rest of the business actually grew. Subscriptions to D-Wave's quantum cloud service increased 50% from a year earlier, and professional services climbed by more than 18%. Because total revenue remained flat overall, falling systems revenue appears to have offset those gains.

Selling physical hardware simply takes time. During the second-quarter 2026 earnings call, management explained that system timing typically depends on site selection. Once a location is finalized, each machine must still be built, installed, and calibrated.

Looking over the latest twelve months, D-Wave's revenue performed worse than flat. Revenue fell 44%, mostly because first-quarter revenue dropped 81% from a year earlier. That is a stark contrast to its three-year average of 37.7% growth a year.

D-Wave's Adjusted EBITDA Loss Has Widened

D-Wave's costs increased during the quarter without a corresponding bump in revenue. D-Wave's adjusted EBITDA loss widened 85% from a year earlier, an expansion management attributed mostly to product development and sales staff expenses. Gross margin also dropped to 55.4% from 63.8% a year earlier, with management again pointing to personnel costs.

The stock has already taken a heavy hit. D-Wave shares lost 59% over the past twelve months, while the S&P 500 returned 17.0%. Despite that drop, the shares still trade at 434.9 times sales, compared to 3.1 for the S&P 500. This valuation likely assumes future revenue will eclipse today's baseline many times over.

D-Wave Expects A Bigger Fourth Quarter

The company does have orders in hand that have not yet converted into revenue. D-Wave's backlog reached $40.7 million on June 30, 2026, up 668% from a year earlier. Management expects about 57% of that backlog to become revenue within twelve months.

Shares of the software maker have appreciated by 7.96% over the course of the past month, outperforming the Computer and Technology sector's gain of 4.85%, and the S&P 500's gain of 2.36%.

It is also important to note the recent changes to analyst estimates for Microsoft. These revisions help to show the ever-changing nature of near-term business trends. With this in mind, we can consider positive estimate revisions a sign of optimism about the business outlook.

Based on our research, we believe these estimate revisions are directly related to near-term stock moves. To capitalize on this, we've crafted the Zacks Rank, a unique model that incorporates these estimate changes and offers a practical rating system.

The Zacks Rank system ranges from #1 (Strong Buy) to #5 (Strong Sell). title: Is Salesforce Still The Business You Bought?
detail:
Is Salesforce Still The Business You Bought?
Trefis Team
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 2:31 PM PDT 3 min read
CRM
MSFT
ORCL
ADBE
NOW
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

If you hold Salesforce (CRM), you likely bought into a subscription software provider known for steady growth and reliable cash generation. During its fiscal Q2 2027 earnings call in August, management noted that a $25 billion accelerated share repurchase was still under way. Has a buyback of that size changed the company behind your shares?

Partly: Salesforce's Balance Sheet Has Changed

While the core software operation looks much as it did a year ago, the underlying balance sheet looks starkly different. Debt accounted for 38.1% of the company's assets during fiscal Q2 2027, the latest reported quarter. For the fourteen years prior to the past year, that metric typically sat around 14.8%. In absolute terms, Salesforce held total debt of $41.7 billion at the end of the quarter. That compares with just $11.4 billion in cash and short-term investments.

Why Is Salesforce's Debt So High?

Salesforce is currently spending more on its own stock than its operations generate. The company deployed $35.1 billion for buybacks over the last twelve months, yet its free cash flow over the same period came in at $15.2 billion. Bridging that shortfall required Salesforce to rely on existing cash reserves or tap debt markets. During the August call, management said it expects to buy back at least 14% of the shares outstanding through the accelerated program.

The underlying business still resembles the enterprise of a year ago. Salesforce recorded an operating margin of 22% over the last twelve months, climbing slightly from 21% a year earlier. Management noted that customer attrition sits near its lowest level ever. Meanwhile, fiscal Q2 2027 revenue grew 11% from a year earlier in constant currency.

What Do You Get For Salesforce's Debt?

Shareholders walk away with a larger slice of the business. Salesforce reported 821 million diluted shares in the latest reported quarter, a drop from 962 million a year earlier. Each remaining share now holds a claim on a larger portion of the profit. The company has also acquired this stock at a discount to current trading levels. Management noted in August that shares purchased so far under the accelerated program cost an average of $176 each, below the $229.13 price where the stock now trades.

The tradeoff comes in the form of the debt Salesforce now carries. After subtracting cash, Salesforce carries debt equal to about 1.8 times a year of its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. The company must service interest on those obligations before any cash can reach shareholders.

title: Should You Sell Your Okta Stock After It Tripled In Six Months?
detail:
Should You Sell Your Okta Stock After It Tripled In Six Months?
Trefis Team

OKTA
^GSPC
MSFT
SAIL
CRWD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pexels

Okta (OKTA) stock has returned 225% over the past six months, far outpacing the S&P 500's 14.4% return. Investors holding the shares are sitting on a large gain, raising the question of whether to hold or take profits. The company sells identity software to more than 20,000 customers, and recent buyers may be betting on its new products designed for AI agents. So how much are you paying today for each dollar Okta earns?

Okta's Thin Margin Helps Explain Its 137x P/E

Investors are currently paying 136.7 times Okta's earnings over the past twelve months, compared with 21.9 times for the S&P 500. That is the company's price-to-earnings ratio. In practical terms, each dollar Okta earns costs about six times what a dollar of the broader index's profit costs.

One reason for that high valuation is Okta's comparatively thin profit margin. The company kept 9.6% of its sales as net profit over the past twelve months, falling short of the 13.3% for the S&P 500. This multiple would come down if Okta's profit grew faster than its share price.

Okta Has Outgrown The S&P 500 Over Three Years

Okta grew revenue 10.6% from a year earlier in its latest quarter. Over the past three years, the company expanded sales by 14.2% a year on average, easily beating the 5.9% growth rate of the S&P 500. While Okta has expanded faster than the broader market over that stretch, the pace may fall short of what investors expect given the stock's current price.

During the fiscal Q2 2027 call in August, management raised its outlook and now expects revenue growth of 10% to 11% for fiscal 2027. That guidance includes about a 1-point headwind from shifting more professional services work to partners. Management also called the period a record for bookings outside a fourth quarter. For fiscal Q3 2027, the company guided to revenue growth of 10%.

Are Okta's AI Agent Products Selling Yet?

Okta's AI agent products are finding buyers, but not yet at a volume that alters the company's financial results. Okta for AI Agents secures the automated agents that customers deploy. While this technology may be exactly what recent buyers of the stock are paying for, the immediate financial impact remains muted. Okta won dozens of AI deals in fiscal Q2 2027, including several worth more than $1 million each. However, management noted on the earnings call that the product is still too small to show up in the numbers.

Management does not expect AI to be material in fiscal 2027. They did flag a real possibility for fiscal 2028 and beyond if current trends continue. The company boasts a larger pipeline of AI deals than it did a quarter earlier, but management cautioned that they cannot yet tell how fast those deals will convert. Okta's wider set of new products is already gaining traction, however. Led by Okta Identity Governance, these offerings made up about 30% of bookings in fiscal Q2 2027.
